name: Tomas Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead seed-traceability software at a tech company, where I am among the best at following a lot-number error. I never use AI tools and check release code against the seed company’s paper register. Greta grows flowers in a small greenhouse, our children are grown, and typical lead pay has helped us rent with three months of expenses saved and some nearby software options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the seed-tracing team that a small AI shortcut may sort a list, but each bag still needs the right lot number. I never use AI tools; I match our code’s label to the seed company’s paper register.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead this system at a tech company; I am good at finding where a seed lot was mislabelled. Greta grows flowers in a small greenhouse, our children are grown, and typical lead pay has helped us rent with about three months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking one lot-label release against the paper register each Monday. We would save 125 monthly while both incomes hold and patch the greenhouse door rather than buy a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about my job and our rent in this picture. A seed bag with the wrong name does not become the right crop because a report looks tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was a lot mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pallet of bean seed carried last season’s lot number, so a grower would have got the wrong planting advice. I caught it by comparing the print file with the register.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why never use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can trace the label back to the record and the person who entered it. I will not sign a bag from an answer I cannot check.

say: I want **seed labels** matched to the paper lot register.
I want **named release checks** before bags leave.
think: I have **three months saved** from typical lead pay and greenhouse flower sales.
I see **rent covered** while my lead wage and actual flower orders continue.
do: **Check lot labels** against paper register every Monday.
**Save 125 monthly** while both incomes hold; patch greenhouse door before replacement.

fieldNote: His **lead skill** is tracing label errors through actual seed records.
The **three-month buffer** supports present security without relying on grown children or future greenhouse sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking buying, checking and coding could handle many seed orders, but someone must still sign for a lot that goes to growers. I would ask management for a written staffing plan before it changes the release desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid lead hours could shrink if one person watches several automated warehouses. Three months saved gives us some time, but Greta’s flower sales cannot replace my full wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the manager this month for written lead hours and approved paid time beside the warehouse checker to learn a physical lot audit. If approved, I’d inspect two sample bags weekly against the register; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local seed-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours, though I trust a physical sample more than a rumour. A bag has to be right before the grower opens it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the printed lot, seal and shelf record on two sample bags. The checker would correct me before I signed anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have not used one, and a sample bag gives me evidence I can show to the warehouse manager.

I want **written lead hours** before warehouses automate.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** if one person oversees several automated seed warehouses.
I cannot use **Greta’s flowers** as a dependable replacement for my developer wage.
do: **Request written hours**; practise sample-bag audits only with approved paid warehouse-checker time.
**Search paid seed-software vacancies** if hours fall and local wages cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious** about own hours and lot errors.
S1.quote: A bag has to be right before the grower opens it.
fieldNote: He chooses **physical sample learning** rather than an AI tool he has never used.
The **paid-time gate** and vacancy wage floor keep the plan tied to current bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write tracing code and check lot registers cheaper than our team. Robots sorting seed bags and tending greenhouses may follow around 2031, after our desk work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the developer team could be cut, including my lead role. Three months saved and Greta’s seasonal sales would not carry rent and bills for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d postpone the planned kitchen cupboards and ask for written notice of any lead cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local seed-warehouse quality openings only if they exist, I meet current handling requirements and wages cover rent and bills; I would not buy machinery for an untested seed business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing the wage we count on. A full greenhouse is not a guaranteed pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Greta expand flower sales?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if customers place and pay for more orders. I would not budget for extra income before it comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for seed work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would check local seed firms and software employers first. Greta’s greenhouse and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach seed records first.
I expect **sorting robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **lead wage** could end quickly when AGI handles lot records.
I know **three months saved** is a short runway for finding local paid work.
do: **Postpone kitchen cupboards** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for warehouse quality** after 2028 loss only if qualified paid local vacancies cover rent and bills.
S2.quote: A full greenhouse is not a guaranteed pay slip.
fieldNote: The **warehouse option** requires current handling rules, actual vacancies and bill-covering wages.
He will not **buy seed machinery** or count unbooked flower orders as income.

steps.text: Postpone planned kitchen cupboards and request written lead-cut notice now
Apply for qualified paid local seed-warehouse vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn which seed-quality checks still require a person at the warehouse. Robots sorting bags and tending greenhouses may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn modern seed sampling while keeping my developer wage, but code expertise is not a handling qualification. I would need paid supervised practice, not a course bought from our three-month buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the seed company and my employer for an approved paid half-day monthly with a qualified warehouse sampler. If both approve and the company funds the current handling course, I’d practise drawing one sample under supervision; we would save 110 monthly while both incomes hold, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local seed-quality vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the code job but glad to learn a proper physical check. A sample bag tells the truth only if I know how to take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the sampler teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sampler would show me which bags to select, how to seal the sample and how to record the lot. I would not sign a quality certificate alone after one lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company refuses funding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer job and not claim a new handling skill. I would not spend rent savings on an unapproved course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives us time to clean up lot records and check the real cost of training. Robots sorting bags and tending greenhouses may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still need paid work at 68 and have not checked a retirement amount. Three months saved makes our rent secure now, but I would not treat a future seed-quality job as certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing lot releases and save 120 monthly while both incomes hold. I’d request a written retirement-income estimate this year; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local seed-quality vacancies only if I complete funded supervised handling training and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about a later job change but secure in the next few years. A record is useful only when the seed in the bag matches it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no funded training exists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid software role while it lasts and consider only vacancies I already qualify for if it ended. I would not call an unfunded warehouse visit training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help in the greenhouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own jobs and homes. Greta and I will plan from orders we actually get, not their labour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could end before a qualified paid local seed-quality job exists. Written notice and a real bill-covering opening would let us use savings carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would buy seed machinery if code work ended. I will not put our rent reserve into seed-processing machinery before a grower agrees to buy its output.

headlineQuote: I will not put our rent reserve into seed-processing machinery before a grower agrees to buy its output.
portrait: Tomas is a **58-year-old software lead** with a master’s degree, typical pay and three months saved.
He and Greta **rent** while greenhouse flower orders vary and grown children live separately.
He **never uses AI** and checks seed labels against paper lot registers.
He considers **paid seed sampling** only with funded handling training, supervision and qualified local vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his lead wage before a paid local seed-quality opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice** and a qualified bill-covering local vacancy would help.
